title: A hard ending, read as allegory
hook: the goldsmith she loves is brought and poisoned; Rumi reads it as a parable of false loves, and literal readers rightly flinch

segments.voice: Yesterday, Avicenna: an older tale echoed as the physician found her secret at Samarkand. Your line was where the pulse leaps.

Old books have stories that are hard to read, where something happens that makes a modern reader put the book down and say, wait, what? You can pretend the passage isn't there. You can throw out the whole book. Or you can do the harder thing: read it closely, notice what the author was doing, and still say honestly, this troubles me. The story of the king and the handmaid ends in a way that can stop a modern reader cold. I'm not going to skip it. Today, a hard ending.
screen: `STORIES THAT MAKE YOU SAY, WAIT.` → `DON'T SKIP IT.` → `A HARD ENDING.`

segments.voice: The physician tells the king: send for the goldsmith in Samarkand, and tempt him with gold and fine robes. The goldsmith comes, proud and delighted, leaving his home and family. The king gives him the girl in marriage. For six months they're happy, and she gets well. Then the physician gives the goldsmith a drink that makes him sicken. His good looks fade, and as his beauty goes, her love goes with it. And he dies. Near the end he says, in effect, my beauty killed me, the way a deer is hunted for its musk. It's grim, and Rumi knows it. He steps in: this was not done out of lust or greed; the physician acted on God's command. He compares it to a story in the Quran, where a mysterious servant of God, whom tradition calls Khidr, kills a boy, and Moses is horrified until he's shown a hidden reason. Sufi commentators have read the whole story as allegory. The king is the spirit, the girl is the soul, and the goldsmith is a love for surfaces, for things that look golden and fade. The physician is the guide who lets that false love run its course until the soul sees through it. In that reading, nobody real is poisoned; an illusion dies. Readers who take it as a story about people rightly flinch: an innocent man is lured from home and killed. Both reactions are honest, and this path doesn't smooth that over. You can learn from what Rumi meant and still say plainly: this is hard to read.
screen: `THE GOLDSMITH IS LURED WITH GOLD.` · `HE FADES, AND HER LOVE FADES.` · `RUMI: DONE AT GOD'S COMMAND.` · `ALLEGORY, AND AN HONEST FLINCH.` · then, large: `HARD TO READ.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a story you grew up with, from a scripture, a family legend, a movie or a fairy tale, that looks different depending on how you read it. Hold the first reading, then the second, without choosing between them yet. Notice what it's like to keep both in your hands, the meaning and the discomfort; that's part of reading old books well.
Khidr, the mysterious servant of God in the Quran whose hidden reasons parallel the physician's hard choice. Today's word.
Your line: hard to read. You can keep both the love and the trouble. Day one hundred seventy-three, done.

howItsDone: Commentators on the Masnavi, from medieval Sufi scholars to modern teachers, have read the end of the king and the handmaid as an allegory of the soul freed from a false love, and some modern readers also name how troubling it is taken literally.
